sections.overview: Actias luna, the luna moth, is a large North American silk moth recognized by its pale green wings and long hindwing tails. It is associated with deciduous and mixed forests where its caterpillars can feed on suitable broadleaf trees. The striking adult is short-lived and does not feed; most growth happens during the caterpillar stage.
sections.identification: The adult has pale lime-green wings, a white to pinkish outer margin, translucent eyespots and a long curved tail on each hindwing. Its wingspan is about 75–105 mm; the sexes are similar in size, while males have more strongly feathered antennae. This combination distinguishes it from Asian Actias species also called moon moths. The cited field references report wingspan but no dependable body-mass range.
sections.habitat: It occurs across much of eastern North America, from parts of Canada through the eastern United States and into northern Mexico. It is associated with deciduous or mixed forest and hardwood swamps, where host trees grow. Brood number and adult flight season vary with latitude: northern populations usually have one generation, while warmer southern areas can have multiple generations.
sections.diet: Caterpillars eat leaves of broadleaf trees and shrubs. Documented hosts include birches in northern populations and, farther south, hickories, walnuts, sumacs, sweetgum and persimmon; host suitability differs among geographic populations. Adults have vestigial mouthparts and do not feed, so nectar is not their food source.
sections.behavior: Adults fly at night and are strongly attracted to light, particularly ultraviolet wavelengths. Males can fly long distances to locate females, which release a sex-attractant pheromone; mating often takes place after midnight. The long hindwing tails may disrupt bat echolocation, a proposed defense supported by experimental research cited by UF/IFAS.
sections.reproduction: Females lay eggs singly or in small groups on host-plant leaves after mating, over several nights. Caterpillars pass through five instars and spin a cocoon among leaves; the cocoon drops with autumn foliage, and the pupa overwinters in the leaf litter. In spring or summer, the adult emerges, dries its wings and then seeks a mate. Development speed depends on temperature and photoperiod.
sections.ecology: Luna moth caterpillars feed on deciduous trees but are not usually abundant enough to cause substantial damage. The adults and caterpillars are prey for other animals; caterpillars are also hosts to parasitoid insects. Their long tails may help adults evade bats, linking their distinctive shape to predator avoidance.
sections.conservation: A global IUCN category was not verified in the sources used for this profile. UF/IFAS notes concern that artificial light at night may disrupt mating and affect populations in urban areas, but this is not a quantified global trend. Habitat quality, suitable host trees and light pollution are relevant local considerations.
